newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Special factors allowable in EMU criteria - Waigel.
newsitem.headline: Special factors allowable in EMU criteria - Waigel.

text.p: German finance minister Theo Waigel said on Monday that a strict interpretation of the criteria for the entry to Economic and Monetary Union still allowed special factors to be taken into account.

Citing a series of special factors which had boosted German debt levels, Waigel told a news conference "it is not the case that it is not allowed to point to such factors within a strict interpretation" of the criteria.
Earlier on Tuesday, Waigel said as he arrived in Brussels to present Germany's convergence programme to other European Union Finance Ministers that special circumstances had boosted German debt.

He cited Germany's high contributions to the European Union, large transfers to east Germany and funds given to eastern European countries. A further boost had come from debt absorbed from the German railways, he said.

The convergence programme, which was approved by other ministers at the meeting, shows German debt at 61.5 percent of gross domestic product this year, above the 60 percent level set as a target in the Maastricht Treaty, which lays down the entry criteria for monetary union.

According to the terms of the Treaty, countries must either be running debt at below this level or be showing considerable progress in moving toward this level. Germany appears to fail on both counts, with its debt above this level and moving higher.
Waigel said that the argument that Germany had faced special burdens had been accepted -- and presented -- by other ministers as important for Germany's case.
Europe plans to create a single currency from 1999 grouping those countries which meet specific economic targets on inflation, interest and exchange rates, debt and public deficits.
A decision on who qualifies will be taken in early 1998. Most nations are finding the most difficulty in meeting the fiscal criteria.
